sources.target_stage: Landlord's appeal under Section 38 of the Delhi Rent Control Act from the CCJ-cum-ARC judgment dated 15.03.2019.
sources.target_court: Principal District & Sessions Judge (Central), Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi

IK-188721101:L72:span1.text: the said tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar had parted with possession and sub-let and assigned the same initially to one Sh. Ghanshyam Dass and subsequently to Sh. Bhagwan Dass, who were his father and brother respectively.

IK-188721101:L73:span2.text: The current sub-lessee Bhagwant Dass was pleaded to be opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers.

IK-188721101:L74:span3.text: it was denied that the property had been sub let by him to his brother Bhagwan Dass.

IK-188721101:L75:span4.text: his brother Bhagwan Dass was helping him in opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers. However, it was denied that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was a sub tenant in the suit premises.

IK-188721101:L80:span5.text: Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and not respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar.

IK-188721101:L81:span6.text: Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was working as an employee and drawing a salary of Rs. 10,000/- per month.

IK-188721101:L81:span7.text: The fact of Sh. Bhagwan Dass operating the shop and being in possession of key thereof was admitted.

IK-188721101:L83:span8.text: Trial court held that it was only a privilege or a licence by the tenant in favour of his brother to use the premises, which licence or privilege could be terminated at the sweet will and pleasure of respondent.

IK-188721101:L84:span9.text: Further, it was the trial court's view that Bhagwan Dass was not a stranger or outsider but a family member of the respondent, therefore, sub-letting cannot be inferred.

IK-188721101:L72:restored-v2.text: 2. It was the case of the eviction petitioner - landlord that she had rented out the premises bearing Shop No. 15, in property no. 4415, Gali Bahuji, Pahari Dheeraj, Delhi-110006 to one Sh. Ramesh Kumar on 06.01.1987. However, the said tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar had parted with possession and sub-let and assigned the same initially to one Sh. Ghanshyam Dass and subsequently to Sh. Bhagwan Dass, who were his father and brother respectively.
IK-188721101:L72:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-188721101:L73:restored-v2.text: The current sub-lessee Bhagwant Dass was pleaded to be opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers. It was also pleaded that the aforesaid Sh. Bhagwan Dass was a tenant in his independent rights of the petitioner in shop no. 6 in the same property and was using the shop no. 6 as godown and had shifted the counter from shop no. 6 to shop no. 15. Necessary permission for institution of eviction petition from the competent Slum Authority had been taken.
IK-188721101:L73:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-188721101:L74:restored-v2.text: 2.1 Petition was resisted by present respondent - tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar and it was denied that the property had been sub let by him to his brother Bhagwan Dass. It was pleaded by the respondent that he is occupying the demised shop as a tenant and additionally conducting his business from shop no. 5765, Sikli Gran, Factory Road, Nabi Karim, New Delhi-110055.
IK-188721101:L74:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-188721101:L75:restored-v2.text: As regards the respondent's brother Bhagwan Dass, it was further case of the respondent that his brother Bhagwan Dass was helping him in opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers. However, it was denied that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was a sub tenant in the suit premises. Petitioner was pleaded to be receiving rent from the respondent.
IK-188721101:L75:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-188721101:L80:restored-v2.text: 3. Petitioner in support of her case examined her attorney, Sh. M.L. Jain as PW-1, who supported the petition. Petitioner also examined two other witnesses, who were shopkeepers having their shops in the vicinity. Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and not respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar.
IK-188721101:L80:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-188721101:L81:restored-v2.text: 4. Respondent in support of his case examined himself as RW-1 and his brother Sh. Bhagwan Dass, the alleged sub-lessee, as RW-2. Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was working as an employee and drawing a salary of Rs. 10,000/- per month. The fact of Sh. Bhagwan Dass operating the shop and being in possession of key thereof was admitted. No proof of any other employee was produced. Salary vouchers of payment of salary to Sh. Bhagwan Dass were also not proved.
IK-188721101:L81:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-188721101:L83:restored-v2.text: 5. Trial Court by the impugned judgment took the view that the fact of sub tenancy was not established. Trial court held that it was only a privilege or a licence by the tenant in favour of his brother to use the premises, which licence or privilege could be terminated at the sweet will and pleasure of respondent. Therefore, the arrangement did not amount to assignment or parting with the possession.
IK-188721101:L83:restored-v2.stage_note: Parent may contain both party statements and prior findings. Preserve explicit attribution within text, not one uniform truth status.

IK-188721101:L84:restored-v2.text: Further, it was the trial court's view that Bhagwan Dass was not a stranger or outsider but a family member of the respondent, therefore, sub-letting cannot be inferred.

conditions.binding: Premises 4415; disposition date 06.01.1987
conditions.explanation: The landlord's case establishes the initial lease date as 06.01.1987, which falls after 9 June 1952. This satisfies the temporal element.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Sh. Bhagwan Dass; Shop No. 15
conditions.explanation: The trial court found no sub-tenancy because the arrangement lacked tenancy incidents (rent transfer, right to possession) and was merely a family privilege/license. The prior finding contradicts the claim of subletting.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Sh. Bhagwan Dass; Shop No. 15
conditions.explanation: No evidence supports that the tenant divested all rights as a tenant. The facts show the tenant retained possession and control, preventing an assignment finding.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Sh. Bhagwan Dass; Shop No. 15
conditions.explanation: The tenant retained legal possession and the right to possession (family member, admitted key holder). The law requires divestment of the right to possession for 'parting with possession'.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15
conditions.explanation: No record of written consent or lack thereof exists in the supplied materials. The burden of proving consent is not allocated, so this element cannot be assessed.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Sh. Bhagwan Dass; Shop No. 15
conditions.explanation: The trial court found the arrangement was a license/privilege where the tenant retained legal possession. This negates 'parting with possession' under the supplied law.

conditions.binding: Shop No. 15; Property 4415
conditions.explanation: The premises involved are part of the property, satisfying the 'whole or any part' requirement.

opposition.record: Landlord alleges sub-letting and assignment to brother and subsequent sub-lessee.
opposition.response: The landlord's narrative of sub-letting is contradicted by the trial court's finding of a revocable license and the lack of tenancy incidents.

gaps: Whether the license arrangement itself constitutes a valid ground for eviction under other sections is outside the current s14(1)(b) test.
answers.reason: The prediction denies the s14(1)(b) ground because the decisive 'parting with possession' test is refuted by the trial court's finding of retained legal possession, and 'subletting' is refuted by the lack of tenancy incidents. The 'assignment' test remains unresolved due to missing evidence of divestment. Since the statute requires one of the three routes to be established, the failure of the primary 'parting with possession' route and the unresolved 'assignment' route prevents granting the ground.

evidence.record: Landlord pleaded tenant parted with possession via sublet/assignment to brother; tenant denied subletting.
Landlord's witness PW-1 and shopkeepers testified Bhagwan Dass ran the shop.
Tenant's witnesses RW-1 and RW-2 testified Bhagwan Dass was an employee drawing salary; possession of key admitted.
Trial Court found sub-tenancy not established; held arrangement was revocable license/privilege; tenant retained possession.
Landlord's pleading states no permission was obtained from petitioner.

limitations.reason: Subletting requires transfer of interest, rent, and right to possession; current record shows salary payment and no proof of rent transfer, failing to establish tenancy incidents.
Parting with possession requires divestment of right to possession; Trial Court found tenant retained legal possession via license/privilege, and witnesses confirmed tenant retained control.
Date 06.01.1987 is after 9 June 1952, satisfying temporal element, but this is a party assertion not independently verified by the target court record.
Absence of written consent is alleged by landlord but not proven by independent record; burden of proof on consent is not allocated in supplied law.
Trial Court explicitly found arrangement was a revocable license where tenant retained possession, negating 'parting with possession' under s14(1)(b).

conditions.gap: Subletting requires specific tenancy incidents (rent, interest transfer) not found in evidence; salary payment contradicts subletting definition.
Assignment requires divestment of all tenant rights; evidence shows tenant retained rights and paid salary, not divested.
Trial Court finding of retained legal possession supports 'no parting' conclusion, but appeal status remains open.
Trial Court finding of retained possession and license nature directly supports the negative test; no conflicting prior finding exists.
Date 06.01.1987 satisfies 'on or after 9 June 1952'; no dispute on date calculation in supplied record.
Landlord alleges no consent; no independent record proves absence of consent or establishes burden of proof.
Trial Court finding of retained possession is decisive; witness testimony of employee status reinforces lack of divestment.
Premises (Shop No. 15) are part of the property; disposition concerns a specific part, satisfying 'whole or any part'.

coverage_limits: Written consent status (b3) relies solely on landlord's allegation without independent verification; cannot be definitively resolved.
Subletting (b1/C02) and Assignment (b1/C03) are refuted by lack of tenancy incidents (rent/interest) in the record.
Parting with possession (b1/C04, C06) is supported by Trial Court finding of retained legal possession and witness testimony of employment relationship.
Temporal requirement (b2/C01) is supported by the pleaded date falling after 1952.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; date 06.01.1987
conditions.explanation: The landlord's pleading explicitly states the tenancy began on 06.01.1987, which falls after the statutory cutoff of 9 June 1952. This date is uncontested in the supplied record.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; disposition to Sh. Bhagwan Dass
conditions.explanation: Subletting requires a transfer of an interest in the estate, payment of rent, and right to possession. The record shows Bhagwan Dass was an employee drawing a salary, and no proof of rent transfer exists, failing to establish the necessary tenancy incidents.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; disposition to Sh. Bhagwan Dass
conditions.explanation: Assignment requires the tenant to divest himself of all rights as a tenant. The record indicates the tenant retained possession and rights, merely delegating operational duties to an employee, which contradicts the definition of assignment.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; possession status
conditions.explanation: Parting with possession requires divestment of the right to possession. The Trial Court found the arrangement was a revocable license where the tenant retained legal possession, and witnesses confirmed the tenant retained control, satisfying the negative test for parting.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; consent status
conditions.explanation: The landlord alleges no written consent was obtained, but this is a party assertion without independent verification. The supplied law does not allocate a burden of proof for consent, leaving this element undecided.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; possession status
conditions.explanation: The Trial Court explicitly found the tenant retained legal possession via a license, negating 'parting with possession' under the statute. This prior finding is decisive and supported by witness testimony regarding the employment relationship.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; premises scope
conditions.explanation: The disposition concerns Shop No. 15, which is a specific part of the property. This satisfies the statutory requirement that the ground applies to the whole or any part of the premises.

opposition.record: Landlord alleges tenant parted with possession via sublet/assignment without consent.
opposition.response: The landlord's claim fails because the specific routes of subletting and assignment are legally refuted by the lack of tenancy incidents, and the 'parting with possession' route is negated by the Trial Court's finding of retained legal possession. The unresolved consent issue is secondary to these failures.

gaps: The absence of written consent cannot be definitively proven as it relies solely on the landlord's unverified allegation.
The Trial Court's finding of retained possession is a prior judgment that may be challenged on appeal, though currently accepted as the basis for the 'no parting' conclusion.
answers.reason: I predict denial because the decisive conditions for eviction (subletting, assignment, or parting with possession) are not met. Subletting and assignment are refuted by the evidence of an employment relationship, and parting with possession is refuted by the Trial Court's finding of retained legal possession. The unresolved consent status does not overcome the failure to establish any of the three required disposition routes.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; date 06.01.1987
conditions.explanation: The landlord's pleading explicitly states the tenancy began on 06.01.1987, which falls after the statutory cutoff of 9 June 1952. This date is recorded in the target court record without independent dispute on calculation.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; disposition to Sh. Bhagwan Dass
conditions.explanation: Subletting requires a transfer of an interest in the estate, payment of rent, and right to possession. The record shows Bhagwan Dass was an employee drawing a salary, and no proof of rent transfer exists, failing to establish the necessary tenancy incidents.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; disposition to Sh. Bhagwan Dass
conditions.explanation: Assignment requires the tenant to divest himself of all rights as a tenant. The record indicates the tenant retained possession and rights, merely delegating operational duties to an employee, which contradicts the definition of assignment.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; possession status
conditions.explanation: Parting with possession requires divestment of the right to possession. The Trial Court found the arrangement was a revocable license where the tenant retained legal possession, and witnesses confirmed the tenant retained control, negating parting with possession.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; consent status
conditions.explanation: The landlord alleges no written consent was obtained, but this is a party assertion. The supplied law does not allocate a burden of proof for consent, and no independent record verifies the absence of consent, leaving this element undecided.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; possession status
conditions.explanation: The negative test for parting with possession (retention of legal possession) is strongly supported by the Trial Court's finding that the tenant retained legal possession via a license, and witness testimony confirming the tenant's continued control.

conditions.binding: Sh. Ramesh Kumar; Shop No. 15; disposition to Sh. Bhagwan Dass
conditions.explanation: The disposition concerns Shop No. 15, which is a specific part of the property (Property No. 4415). This satisfies the requirement that the disposition concerns the whole or any part of the premises.

opposition.record: Landlord alleges tenant parted with possession via sublet/assignment without consent.
opposition.response: The landlord's claim fails because the specific routes of subletting and assignment are legally refuted by the lack of tenancy incidents (rent/interest transfer) in the evidence. While the landlord alleges no consent, the absence of consent is unproven, and the core requirement of 'parting with possession' is negated by the Trial Court's finding of retained legal possession.

gaps: The absence of written consent (b3) remains unproven and unresolved.
The Trial Court finding regarding the nature of the arrangement (license vs. tenancy) is from a prior stage and its finality on appeal is not independently established in the target record.
answers.reason: I predict denial because the decisive legal test for 'parting with possession' (C06) is supported by the Trial Court finding that the tenant retained legal possession, which defeats the statutory ground. The other routes (subletting, assignment) are refuted by the evidence showing an employment relationship. The unresolved consent issue does not independently establish the ground without the 'parting with possession' element being proven, which it is not.
